html:
The ten years of campaigns, from 230 to 221 BCE, in which the state of Qin conquered the six other great states of China: Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and Qi. When Qi fell in 221 BCE, one ruler held all of China for the first time.

The Zhou kings had long been figureheads. For two centuries the Warring States fought each other with ever larger armies. Qin, on the western edge, pulled ahead. Its Legalist reforms, argued for by thinkers like Han Fei, tied land, rank and reward to service to the state, and its armies were the best organised of the age.

The King of Qin, Ying Zheng, took each rival in turn:

  • Han in 230 BCE
  • Zhao in 228 BCE
  • Wei in 225 BCE
  • Chu in 223 BCE
  • Yan in 222 BCE
  • Qi in 221 BCE

He then called himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor. He did away with the old system of hereditary fiefs and ruled through commanderies run by appointed officials. He standardised script, coins, weights and axle widths, and joined older frontier walls into the first Great Wall.

The Qin dynasty itself lasted only fifteen years. But the idea it made real, one empire ruled from one court, outlived it. The Han kept most of the Qin system, and for the next two thousand years unity was the normal state that Chinese rulers tried to restore.
